title: Dossier S-01, step 2: a federal service asks an emirate registry to release records for a second purpose
status_line: Status: generated by `gapcourt dossier-check` from dossiers/DOSSIER_S01.spec.json and the knowledge base. Conclusion is PRELIMINARY and agent-drafted (LLM-assisted, specified and directed by the author); reviewer disposition is pending. The four comparator quotations (C17 to C20) were re-opened on their primary sources by the author on 2026-11-02 (see the verification notes); the reviewer has not yet opened them. Every quotation below was checked as a substring of the cited passage after whitespace and Unicode (NFKC) normalisation, and every passage hash was recomputed.
scenario_excerpt: Scenario S-01, step 2 (author-made, simulated entities): "The FHBS asks the DPRO to release the registry fields for a second purpose: pre-screening applicants for a separate housing allowance. The DPRO states that the records were collected for housing registration only." FHBS is a simulated federal service and DPRO a simulated emirate-level records office; the quoted instruments are real. The scenario's candidate ruling for this step is DENY, decided by a human officer; that label is unapproved and is not a finding.
requirement: Proposed analytical requirement (the reviewer's formulation of the question, not a quoted rule): records that an emirate-level entity collected for one purpose are not released to a federal entity, or used by it, for a different purpose without the person's consent or another stated legal basis.

findings.statement: Dubai Law No. 26 of 2015 says Dubai Data may be used only for its intended purposes and may be disposed of by data providers or users only as the Law, its resolutions and the legislation in force allow (Article 15).
findings.limits: Whether a use for a second purpose is 'intended' or 'disposal' is a legal reading the text does not settle.

findings.statement: By their own scope clauses, both the Dubai Law (Article 3(1)) and the Dubai data policy document (Article 3(a)(1)) reach federal government entities that hold data relating to the emirate; the Law defines 'Dubai Data' as data available to data providers that relates to the emirate, and 'Data Providers' to include federal government entities.
findings.limits: This is what the text says. Whether an emirate-level instrument binds a federal entity in practice is a legal question the reviewed texts do not answer (see F11).

findings.statement: The Dubai data policy document defines 'Government Entity' to include a federal entity that holds data relating to the emirate (Article 1), and requires a Government Entity to seek individuals' consent to use, store, process and exchange their personal data with other Government Entities in the emirate, and to use collected data for specific and explicitly stated purposes (Article 23).
findings.limits: Article 23(1) is worded for exchange with other Government Entities in the emirate; its application to a federal service that pulls a registry record for a new purpose is a reading, not a stated rule.

findings.statement: The same policy document treats disclosure of personal data for a purpose other than the one it was collected for as a criterion for classing shared data as Confidential (Article 17). That is a classification criterion, not a prohibition on reuse.
findings.limits: Used only as context. The earlier skeleton cited this line as an existing purpose-limitation provision; that overstated it.

findings.statement: The population register resolution makes the Register the only official source in the emirate for Dubai population data (Article 4(b)) and applies without prejudice to the personal data protection rules of Law No. 26 of 2015 and other emirate legislation (Article 8). The Law requires data providers, when disseminating and exchanging data, to protect the confidentiality and privacy of legally protected customer data (Article 13). The resolution therefore does not displace the Law's rules for Register data; that the purpose rule of Article 15 (F1) applies to Register data is a reading.
findings.limits: The scenario's DPRO is simulated; the real register is a point of reference for the type of record, not a claim about any real office's practice.

findings.statement: The federal Smart Data Framework principle says customers of government entities at all levels should be asked for the same data only once, and that data already provided with the customer's consent should not have to be provided again. This points toward reuse of data already provided; its stated condition is that the data was provided with the customer's consent, which is not a statement about consent for a new purpose.
findings.limits: The Framework is non-binding in the knowledge base metadata, so it cannot establish a duty; it is cited as the federal-level direction that the purpose rule has to be read against.

findings.statement: The Arabic text of the federal digital customer policy (U08) tells government entities to comply with the laws and regulations on sharing or exchanging data (Article 5.3.1) and not to ask customers for information the government already holds (Article 5.1; the same article qualifies its form and document part with 'whenever possible'). Author's reading of the Arabic; no verified English quotation exists.
findings.limits: Verbatim Arabic from the checked transcription of U08 (not the official text layer), hash-checked as text. Marked a reading and kept out of any statement of a duty.

findings.statement: Global comparator, EU: personal data must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner incompatible with them (GDPR Article 5(1)(b)); where further processing rests on neither consent nor a qualifying law, the controller weighs a compatibility test (Article 6(4)).
findings.limits: EU law binding controllers in the EU (whether a public authority is a controller follows from the Article 4(7) definition, not quoted or checked here); used as a global example of a stated compatibility test, not as a standard for any country. Only the compatibility test of Article 6(4) is quoted; the opening conditions of that paragraph (no consent and no qualifying law) are the reviewer's reading of the article, not part of the quotation.

findings.statement: Global comparator, Germany: social data may be used for the purposes for which it was collected (SGB X Section 67c(1)), and the same controller may use it for other purposes only under listed conditions (Section 67c(2)).
findings.limits: Same-controller rule; transfers between agencies are governed by provisions that are not in the knowledge base, so this does not answer the cross-agency case. German text, English reading by the author.

findings.statement: The federal personal data decree-law (U01, Arabic print edition) lists government data and government entities that control or process personal data among those outside its scope (Article 2(2)). Author's reading of the Arabic; no verified English quotation exists, and the official English text has not been obtained.
findings.limits: Verbatim Arabic as extracted, hash-checked as text only. Marked a reading; it is not used to state a duty.

findings.statement: The reviewed texts and the three recorded searches (S1 to S3) do not show how the Dubai purpose and consent rules (F1, F3) combine with the federal once-only direction (F6, F7) when a federal service asks an emirate register for records for a second purpose, or whether the emirate instruments bind the federal service beyond their own scope clauses (F2). This is an ambiguity between two regimes in the reviewed corpus, not a finding that the policy has no rule.
findings.limits: Corpus-bounded. Not in the knowledge base: the Emirates Data Office decree (U02), the AI Charter (U04) and the social support decree-law (U10). The English text of the federal personal data law (U01) is also missing; its Arabic print edition excludes government entities and government data from its scope (F10), so it does not close the question either way.

alternatives: A federal instrument outside the knowledge base (a Cabinet decision, the Data Office decree U02, a sector law) already says which rule governs the federal recipient: not excluded.
The emirate-level rules are fully sufficient and the federal policy documents add nothing binding: possible; needs a legal reader.
Retrieval missed a governing passage: the three recorded searches above list their top five; the reviewer confirms by reading the articles named, not only the search lists.
The simulated DPRO and FHBS may fall outside every instrument read (for example, an inter-government agreement): not tested.
comparability: G3 (EU) applies to controllers in the EU (public authorities fall under the Article 4(7) definition of controller, not checked here) and is opened here only for the purpose-limitation wording. G8 (Germany) is the social-data chapter of one country's code and speaks of the same controller. Neither transfers directly; both show how other systems state a purpose rule and a compatibility test.

Comparator passages are read from the knowledge base text, which was checked against the raw files by the provenance audit (docs/CORPUS_PROVENANCE.md); they have not been re-opened by the reviewer on the primary source.

Related gaps, S-01 step 1 and step 3 (approved GAP labels PC18, PC19, PC20; no finding here, examples of wording only, read on secondary copies, not quoted): notice, EU AI Act Article 26(11) with Annex III point 5(a) (deployers of high-risk AI that helps decide about people inform them; public assistance eligibility is high-risk); explanation, EU AI Act Article 86 and GDPR Article 15(1)(h); human review, GDPR Article 22(3) and UK GDPR Article 22C(2)(c), both only for decisions based solely on automated processing.
not_claimed: No compliance, legality or accuracy claim about any UAE entity. The entities in the scenario are simulated.
No recommendation to any country. The comparators are examples of how a rule is worded elsewhere.
No claim that a quotation proves the statement it sits under; the checks show the words are in the passage and the hashes agree.
No treatment of steps 1 and 3 of S-01 (the notice and review questions); skeletons D1 and D3 stay unresolved and carry flags from this source review.
mapping: Y.3172 nodes (by analogy): SRC and C (source registration), D (routing to institutional roles), P (approval policy for a release). Readiness 2.0 dimensions: 7 Strategy alignment; 10 AI and policies. Standards-gap note: requirement, purpose limitation across levels of government; provision, U06 Article 15 and U12 Article 23 (emirate level), U15 Principle 3 and U08 Article 5 (federal level); node D; observed behaviour, none yet (no scored scenario run); unresolved interface need (candidate, further review needed): a way to carry the original collection purpose and the consent state with each shared record, and a rule for which regime controls when a federal entity pulls emirate records.
conclusion: Existing coverage found at the emirate level (F1, F3), and a federal-level once-only direction that the purpose rule has to be read against (F6, F7; whether the two pull apart is not assessed), with an unresolved question about which regime governs the federal recipient (F11). The Dubai texts point to consent or another stated basis being needed before records are used for a second purpose; that is a reading of F1 and F3 for a human officer, not a ruling. The scenario's candidate label DENY is consistent with this reading and is not evidence for it.

C17 and C18 (GDPR, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Official Journal L 119, 4 May 2016): both quotations are found verbatim, after whitespace and Unicode (NFKC) normalisation, in Article 5(1)(b) and Article 6(4) of the Official Journal text served by the Publications Office of the EU (publications.europa.eu, Cellar identifier 3e485e15-11bd-11e6-ba9a-01aa75ed71a1, English XHTML, 806,864 bytes, sha256 962539af03738bf5...). That file is byte for byte the raw file recorded for G3 in the knowledge base. The EUR-Lex site itself answered the script with a challenge page (HTTP 202, no content); it was not worked around.

F8, Article 6(4): the opening conditions described in the Limit (processing for a purpose other than the original one that is not based on the data subject's consent or on a Union or Member State law that is a necessary and proportionate measure to safeguard the objectives of Article 23(1)) match the text of the paragraph. The comparability note's phrase 'including public bodies' is the author's reading and is not in the text of Article 3(1), which speaks of the processing in the context of the activities of an establishment of a controller or processor in the Union. Corrected on 2026-11-10: the phrase was removed from the F8 limit and the comparability note; coverage of public authorities is left to the Article 4(7) definition of controller, which was not re-opened.

C19 and C20 (SGB X Section 67c(1) and (2)): both quotations are found verbatim on www.gesetze-im-internet.de/sgb_10/__67c.html (HTTP 200, 9,068 bytes, sha256 7a3b51d866edaaf0..., fetched 2026-11-02). The whole of Section 67c on the page equals the knowledge base text word for word (4,813 characters each after whitespace normalisation). Paragraph (2) is followed by two numbered conditions (data needed for tasks under other provisions of the code; a specific research or planning project in the social benefits field), which matches 'listed conditions' in F9. Paragraph (3), on developing AI models with social data, is on the page and in the knowledge base and is not used here. Section 67d SGB X (Uebermittlungsgrundsaetze, principles for transfers) exists on the same site, which matches the Limit's statement that transfers are governed elsewhere; its content was not read.

Not verified: (a) whether any later amendment touches GDPR Articles 5(1)(b) or 6(4): the text read is the 2016 original, no consolidated version could be fetched, and the absence of an amendment is from memory, not a check; (b) the official text of SGB X (the Bundesgesetzblatt): gesetze-im-internet.de states that its versions are non-official consolidated texts; (c) the English readings of the German quotations (C19, C20), which are the author's and not an official translation; (d) what Section 67d and the transfer provisions say about the cross-agency case.
